 Where Indiana candidates will spend election night
 By Casey Smith - Tuesday November 3, 2026 1:00 pm 
 As polls close across Indiana on Tuesday, candidates, party leaders and supporters will gather at election night watch parties to follow returns in races for Congress, statewide offices and the Indiana General Assembly.
 Both major political parties will hold their statewide election night gatherings in downtown Indianapolis, just steps apart.
 The Indiana GOP will host its watch party at the InterContinental Indianapolis, 17 W. Market St., with doors opening at 6 p.m. in the hotel’s ballroom.
 The event will feature the Republican statewide ticket, including secretary of state nominee Max Engling, State Comptroller Elise Nieshalla and State Treasurer Daniel Elliott, along with other Republican candidates, elected officials and supporters.
 The Indiana Democratic Party will gather at the Hilton Indianapolis, 120 W. Market St., in the hotel’s ninth-floor Victory Ballroom.
 Democratic candidates and party officials expected to attend include state party chair Karen Tallian, secretary of state nominee Beau Bayh and state treasurer candidate Coumba Kebe.
 Indiana GOP Chair Randy Head takes a selfie with Governor-elect Mike Braun onstage in Indianapolis on Nov. 6, 2024. (Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle) 
 Independent Indiana Secretary of State Candidate Greg Ballard will host an Indianapolis watch party at locally-owned Visionloft Mass Ave., 235 N. Delaware St. The party for supporters officially begins at 6 p.m. after the polls close in central Indiana.
 The Libertarian Party of Indiana will gather at Switchboard, 801 Shelby St., in Indianapolis, for an election night viewing party. The event begins at 7 p.m., with attendees planning to follow live results throughout the evening.
 Elsewhere across the state, county party organizations are hosting their own gatherings.
 Vanderburgh County Democrats will watch returns at City View at Sterling Square, 210 N. Fulton Ave., in Evansville, beginning at 6 p.m. Dearborn County Democrats have scheduled a gathering at Strong’s Brick Oven Pizzeria in Lawrenceburg from 7 to 11 p.m.
 In Northwest Indiana, Porter County Republicans will gather at Aberdeen Manor in Valparaiso, beginning at 6:30 p.m. Central, to watch election returns.
 The Libertarian Party of Floyd County will also host a watch party at New Albany Tavern, beginning at 6 p.m.
 Polls close at 6 p.m. local time across Indiana, but voters already in line at that time are permitted to cast ballots. Results will begin coming in afterward, with some races potentially remaining undecided late into the night.

 Engling casts ballot — is counting on turnout from Republicans
 By Tom Davies - 12:07 pm 
 Republican secretary of state candidate Max Engling says his dash in less than six months from starting his campaign to reaching Election Day was “an awesome experience” but also “a little surreal.” 
 Engling and his wife Kelcey brought along their four children as they voted Tuesday morning at their precinct voting site near Cicero in rural northern Hamilton County.
 Republican secretary of state candidate Max Engling walks from a voting machine with two of his daughters after casing his ballot at the White River Township Community Building near Cicero, Indiana, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle) 
 Engling told reporters afterward “we know that if Republicans come out and vote, that we will win.”
 He entered the race in May, six months or more after other candidates had jumped in.
 “It’s humbling to be on the ballot,” he said. “We’re running very hard to make sure that we can serve Hoosiers, but yes, we’ve run a whirlwind of a race.”
 Democratic nominee Beau Bayh and Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard both cast early in-person votes last week. Libertarian Lauri Shillings is the fourth candidate on the ballot.
 Despite polls showing a sour mood in the state and nationwide toward President Donald Trump and Republicans, Engling expressed optimism for the Indiana GOP ticket.

 Have questions on Election Day? These hotlines can help.
 By Leslie Bonilla Muñiz - 11:00 am 
 Did you know the state of Indiana has a hotline for voters in need?
 If you have questions or concerns while voting, poll workers on site can help. Counties also typically staff up their own election board phone lines.
 For instance, with federal election observers conducting exit interviews in Lake and Marion counties, officials there recommend dropping them a line: dial 219-755-3795 for the Lake County Election Board or 317-327-VOTE for the Marion County election hotline.
 But one government phone number works for statewide assistance: 866-461-VOTE. That’s the Hoosier Voter Hotline, operated by the Indiana Election Division.
 For help outside the government or in other languages, voters can try a hotline staffed with trained legal volunteers from the Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights.
 For English, use 866-OUR-VOTE, and for Spanish, use 888-VE-Y-VOTA. The hotline is also offered in a variety of Asian languages (888-API-VOTE ) and in Arabic (844-YALLA-US).
 Last updated: 11:02 AM
 Early voting shatters 2022 totals
 By Niki Kelly - 9:53 am 
 More than 755,000 Hoosiers voted early in person statewide — an increase of 40% from four years ago.  
 That’s according to an Indiana Election Division report run Monday afternoon. The number could still grow, as counties finish reporting. In the 2022 midterms, about 538,000 Hoosiers voted early in person.  
 Indiana had nearly 4.8 million residents on the rolls after the Oct. 5 registration deadline. Early voting began the day after. 
 When combined with returned mail ballots, traveling board votes and email votes, almost 848,000 Hoosiers had voted as of Monday, which is far above the 689,000 absentee votes cast in 2022 — and represents about 45% of the roughly 1.9 million vote total that election.
 The Marion County Clerk’s Office on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle) 
 Indiana law refers to both mail-in ballots and early in-person voting as “absentee” votes.  
 While it’s too early to know if this year’s turnout will eclipse previous years, Indiana traditionally has one of the worst turnout rates in the country. The 2020 general election hit a recent high-water mark of 65%, buoyed by an unusual election year with additional absentee voting flexibility, but sank to 40% in 2022’s midterm contest. In 2024, a presidential year, turnout was 62%. 
 According to the Monday report, about 7,100 disabled or injured Hoosiers — or their caretakers — had already voted by traveling board. Bipartisan teams deliver ballots to such voters and help them complete ballots if they’re not physically able to so themselves. 
 About 2,700 Hoosiers had voted by email. No one voted by fax.  
 More than 14,000 would-be voters still hadn’t returned their mail ballots to county clerks, which must be received by 6 p.m. today.

 const getRelativeTime = (current, target) => {
 const timeDiff = Math.floor((target - current) / 1000);
 const relativeTime = new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat('en', {
 numeric: 'always',
 });
 if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60) { // Within minute
 return relativeTime.format(Math.min(Math.round(timeDiff), 1), 'second');
 } else if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60 * 60) { // Within hour
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / 60), 'minute');
 } else if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60 * 60 * 24) { // Within day
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / (60 * 60)), 'hour');
 } else if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60 * 60 * 24 * 7) { // Within week
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / (60 * 60 * 24)), 'day');
 } else if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60 * 60 * 24 * 30) { // Within month
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / ( 60 * 60 * 24 * 7)), 'week');
 } else if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60 * 60 * 24 * 365) { // Within year
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / ( 60 * 60 * 24 * 30)), 'month');
 } else { // Year+
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / (60 * 60 * 24 * 365)), 'year');
 }
 }
